public_rationale: He says that despite promises AI would get cheaper, 'costs have only ever increased' for both providers and customers. This is an absolute claim, so one documented price cut contradicts it. On 2025-06-10, OpenAI cut the price of the same o3 model by 80%, from $10/$40 to $2/$8 per million tokens (e1). In November 2025, Anthropic priced Opus 4.5 at $5/$25 per million tokens (e2). That is two-thirds below the $15/$75 that e1 lists for Opus 4. This is the same tier but a newer model. A survey covering the field to February 2026 reports benchmark cost per task falling 390x in a year (e3). Its authors say this largely reflects reduced test-time parallelism. Anthropic's total compute cost rose from $3.4 billion in Q1 2026 to $5.6 billion in Q2 2026 (e4). That fits a total-spending reading but does not show unit costs rising. On the contract's unit-price reading, the o3 cut alone contradicts the claim for customers.
limitations: If 'costs' means total spending rather than unit prices, the result could differ.
The evidence does not show providers' unit costs, such as cost per token served.
The Opus comparison is between two different models in the same tier. It uses Anthropic's announcement and an earlier third-party record of the old price.
The per-task cost fall in e3 compares different models and largely reflects less parallel compute.
'Calamitously expensive' is a judgment and is not scored.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI is extremely expensive, and its costs for both providers and customers have only ever risen despite promises that they would fall.

statement.excerpt: AI is calamitously expensive and, despite years of promises of it getting cheaper for both those running AI services and its customers, costs have only ever increased.

from_speaker: despite years of promises of it getting cheaper
for both those running AI services and its customers
our_interpretation: 'Calamitously expensive' is a judgment and is not scored.

The checkable part is the absolute statement that costs 'have only ever increased', set against promises of AI 'getting cheaper'. Plain reading for customers: the price paid for comparable AI use (per token for the same or equivalent model, or per task) never fell. A documented price cut for the same model or capability tier contradicts 'only ever increased'.
'Years of promises' points to roughly the period since ChatGPT's launch. I use 2023-01-01 to the post date.
Total spending, as opposed to unit price, is a possible alternative reading. It is noted in the flags.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence that, from 2023 to the post date, the prices customers paid for comparable AI use and providers' unit costs only rose, with no meaningful cuts.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A dated, documented decrease in price for the same or comparable model or task within the period.

evidence.excerpt: OpenAI just dropped the price of their o3 model by 80% - from $10/million input tokens and $40/million output tokens to just $2/million and $8/million for the very same model.
evidence.explanation: Customers' price for the very same model fell 80%. That directly contradicts 'costs have only ever increased' for customers.

evidence.excerpt: Pricing is now $5/$25 per million tokens—making Opus-level capabilities accessible to even more users, teams, and enterprises.
evidence.explanation: Anthropic cut its Opus-tier API price to $5/$25 per million tokens, from the $15/$75 for Opus 4 recorded in e1's source. The price of top-tier Claude use fell by two-thirds.

evidence.excerpt: Cost fell 390x in one year (o3's $4,500/task to GPT-5.2's $12/task), although this largely reflects reduced test-time parallelism.
evidence.explanation: Measured per-task cost on a benchmark fell sharply within a year. The authors note that the fall partly reflects less parallel compute.

evidence.excerpt: The cost of the computing power that runs its Claude models rose far less, to $5.6 billion from $3.4 billion.
evidence.locator: Live update, Oct 26, 2026, 3:53 PM UTC entry
evidence.explanation: A provider's total compute cost rose from Q1 to Q2 2026. That fits the total-spending reading of his claim, though it does not show that unit costs rose.
